blogs.title: Navigating the Ciminelli-Kousisis Divide: Why the Fifth Circuit Got the Scheme-to-Defraud Element Right in Constantinescu
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Fifth Circuit's careful distinction between the Supreme Court's recent decisions in Ciminelli (rejecting the right-to-control theory) and Kousisis (upholding the fraudulent-inducement theory). The court found that the pump-and-dump indictment alleged a classic fraudulent-inducement scheme—tricking victims into parting with money by buying securities—rather than merely depriving them of valuable economic information. The post examines whether this distinction is administrable in practice, whether lower courts are drawing the Ciminelli/Kousisis line consistently, and what the decision signals about the boundaries of federal fraud law after the Supreme Court's recent constriction efforts.

blogs.title: Profit Without Harm: Constantinescu and the Growing Reach of Fraudulent-Inducement Theory After Kousisis
blogs.description: This post focuses on the intent-to-defraud element and the Fifth Circuit's application of Kousisis's holding that fraud does not require the victim to suffer a net economic loss. The defendants argued they intended only to profit, not to harm their followers, who received market-value securities in exchange for their money. The court rejected this argument, treating the intent to obtain money through deception as sufficient. The post explores the doctrinal implications of severing fraud from net-loss requirements, the tension with traditional common-law fraud notions of reliance and damages, and whether this expansion risks criminalizing ordinary commercial puffery or aggressive sales tactics.

blogs.title: From Boiler Rooms to Group Chats: Social Media Pump-and-Dump Schemes and the Adaptability of Traditional Fraud Statutes
blogs.description: This post examines the factual context of Constantinescu—social media influencers using their followings to orchestrate pump-and-dump schemes—and what it reveals about how federal fraud statutes apply to modern, decentralized fraud. Unlike traditional securities fraud cases involving broker-dealers or corporate insiders, here the alleged fraudsters were social-media personalities with no fiduciary relationship to their followers. The post considers whether the absence of a fiduciary duty matters under § 1348, how the case fits into a broader trend of DOJ prosecuting influencer-driven fraud, and whether existing statutes are adequate or whether new regulatory frameworks are needed for social-media-era securities manipulation.

blogs.title: Statutory Borrowing as Constitutional Adjudication: Section 1348's Reliance on Mail and Wire Fraud Precedent
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Fifth Circuit's observation that § 1348 'borrows key concepts from the mail and wire fraud statutes' and that courts routinely rely on mail and wire fraud cases when construing securities fraud. The post examines the implications of this cross-statutory interpretive approach: Does it impermissibly expand § 1348 beyond its text by importing doctrines developed under different statutory schemes? Does it create circularity problems, given that mail and wire fraud statutes themselves have been constrained by Ciminelli? The post also considers whether this borrowing is consistent with fair-notice principles, given that defendants charged under § 1348 may not anticipate the application of mail-fraud jurisprudence.
